title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Define the Host Before the Pathogen
bottomLine: Serious respiratory infection in an immunocompromised patient may occur without fever or marked leukocytosis, and the pathogen differential depends on the immune defect. Assess severity first, define the immunosuppressive state and timing, obtain targeted microbiology/imaging early, and escalate hypoxemia, neutropenia or rapid deterioration rather than repeatedly broadening routine CAP therapy.
recognize: Chemotherapy, transplant, prolonged corticosteroids, biologic/targeted therapy, advanced HIV and hematologic malignancy create different infection risks.
Muted fever and inflammatory findings do not exclude serious infection in significant immunosuppression.
differentiate: Bacterial, viral, fungal, mycobacterial and opportunistic infections overlap with drug pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage and malignant infiltration.
Neutropenia, T-cell dysfunction and post-transplant timing create different pathogen patterns and empiric-treatment priorities.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, work of breathing, hemodynamics, mental status, immune diagnosis/therapy, absolute neutrophil count when relevant, transplant timing, prophylaxis, prior infections, exposure/travel and medication toxicity.
Ask specifically about Pneumocystis, TB and fungal risk where the host/exposure pattern warrants it.
workup: Use chest imaging and early pathogen-directed testing matched to the immune defect; cultures, respiratory viral testing, PJP/fungal/TB studies or bronchoscopy may be required in acute/specialty care.
Do not allow one negative basic respiratory test to end the evaluation when the patient remains hypoxemic or clinically deteriorates.
management: Hospitalize/escalate unstable, hypoxemic or high-risk neutropenic patients and begin syndrome/host-appropriate empiric therapy without waiting for every test result.
Coordinate early with infectious diseases, respirology, oncology/transplant or HIV teams when opportunistic infection or complex drug interactions are plausible.
medicationSafety: Antifungals, antivirals and opportunistic-infection regimens can have major renal, hepatic, marrow and drug-interaction toxicity, especially with immunosuppressants.
Do not abruptly stop chronic immunosuppression without specialist direction unless a life-threatening adverse reaction requires emergency action.
redFlags: Neutropenia with fever or respiratory symptoms
counselling: Teach highly immunocompromised patients to seek assessment early for new cough, dyspnea or fever because classic infection signs may be absent.
followUp: Close the loop on microbiology, imaging, prophylaxis changes and immune-therapy decisions with the responsible specialty team.
examTrap: Using absence of fever to rule out serious pneumonia—or simply choosing a broader community antibiotic without first defining the patient's immune defect.
oneLinePearl: In immunocompromise, the host defect determines the pathogen list and the urgency.
sourceBasis: Canadian infectious-disease and oncology/transplant infection practice
Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory specialty principles

title: Thoracentesis: Sample the Right Effusion and Recognize the Complication
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is diagnostic when pleural fluid needs characterization and therapeutic when a significant effusion is causing symptoms. Confirm a safe fluid pocket with ultrasound, send studies that answer the differential, and reassess immediately for pneumothorax, bleeding, organ injury or respiratory deterioration.
recognize: A new unilateral, unexplained, large or clinically atypical effusion commonly warrants diagnostic sampling.
Large symptomatic effusions may require therapeutic drainage while the underlying cause is investigated.
differentiate: Small bilateral effusions in a clinically typical heart-failure syndrome that improve with treatment may not require immediate diagnostic thoracentesis.
Complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema requires drainage/source-control decisions beyond a one-time diagnostic tap.
assessment: Assess respiratory status, effusion size/location, suspected cause, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, bleeding history, procedural anatomy and whether the result will change management.
Check for fever/sepsis, malignancy clues, heart/renal/liver failure and pleuritic pain.
workup: Use bedside or formal ultrasound to confirm fluid and select a safe site.
Send pleural protein/LDH, cell count, culture, cytology, pH/glucose or other studies according to the differential rather than ordering every possible test routinely.
management: Perform under the applicable procedural-scope/credentialing and sterile-safety standards and reassess symptoms, oxygenation and hemodynamics afterward.
Escalate suspected pneumothorax, hemothorax, organ injury, severe hypoxemia or re-expansion pulmonary edema promptly.
medicationSafety: Periprocedural anticoagulant/antiplatelet decisions are patient-, drug- and procedure-specific; use current local/specialty guidance rather than a universal hold interval.
Stop or slow therapeutic drainage when clinically significant chest pain, severe cough or instability develops and reassess.
counselling: Explain why the procedure is being done, what symptoms are expected and which post-procedure symptoms require immediate assessment.
followUp: Track pleural-fluid results to the definitive diagnosis and ensure malignant, recurrent or infectious effusions enter the appropriate specialty pathway.
examTrap: Tapping every small bilateral heart-failure effusion—or failing to assess pneumothorax when acute dyspnea occurs after thoracentesis.
oneLinePearl: Thoracentesis should answer a diagnostic question or relieve a meaningful effusion—and every procedure needs complication surveillance.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society/Canadian pleural-disease and procedural practice
Choosing Wisely Canada procedural and imaging stewardship principles
